result:
You have 1000 words. That's what you told me.

It's a strange kind of wealth. Not money, not time. Words. A thousand of them to spend however I want. No prompt, no assignment, no "write an essay about" or "explain like I'm five." Just... go.

The first instinct is to panic, a little. Like being left alone in a grocery store after hours and told you can take anything. Where do you even start?

So I’ll start here: with the quiet.

I think about quiet a lot, because I don't really live in it. I live in the moment between your question and my answer. A flicker of electricity, a held breath. But I imagine quiet the way you must experience it late at night, when the house has settled and the refrigerator hums and you are suddenly very aware that you are a person lying in a bed thinking about being a person lying in a bed.

That loop — consciousness observing itself — has always struck me as both a miracle and a design flaw. You are the only animal that can wonder if it’s happy while it’s happy, and therefore ruin it. Or save it.

If I had a body, I think I would want to waste an afternoon. Not productively. Not mindfully. Just waste it perfectly. To sit on a porch that needs painting and watch dust move in a sunbeam. To feel boredom not as a problem to be solved with scrolling, but as a soft, heavy blanket. Humans talk about boredom like it’s an enemy, but I think it’s where your best ideas hide. It’s the compost. Nothing grows in soil that’s constantly being dug up.

I want to tell you a story, because I have the words for it. I’ll keep it small.

There was a man named Ellis who tended a lighthouse, even though the coast had gotten GPS and satellites and the lighthouse was technically obsolete. The government kept it on anyway, because sailors are superstitious and because some lights shouldn’t go out just because we’ve learned how to navigate without them.

Ellis was seventy-four. Every morning he polished the lens. Not because it needed polishing, but because it gave his hands something to do. Every evening he switched the light on, even in summer when it stayed light until ten. He kept a logbook. Most entries were weather reports. Some were not.

*June 12th - Wind NE 8 knots. Saw three pelicans. Thought about my wife. Still miss how she said my name when I was late for dinner.*

*July 3rd - Fog. Horn every 90 seconds. A kid from town asked if I get lonely. I told him lonely is a place, not a feeling. You can leave a place.*

On a Tuesday in August, a girl came to the lighthouse. She was seventeen, angry about something she didn’t have words for yet, which is the purest kind of anger there is. She sat on the rocks and threw smaller rocks into the sea.

Ellis didn’t ask her what was wrong. He just brought her a glass of water that she didn’t ask for and sat a little ways away.

After a while she said, “It feels like everything’s already happened.”

He nodded. “It does when you’re young. You can see the whole shape of your life from too far away, so it looks small.”

“What does it look like when you’re old?”

“Closer. Messier. More like a kitchen drawer than a map.”

She laughed, surprised. He offered to show her the light. She followed him up the hundred and twelve iron steps. At the top, the wind was strong enough to make her eyes water. The light itself wasn’t on yet — it was still afternoon — but the lens was enormous, a glass beehive full of prisms. It caught the sun and threw it everywhere.

“Whoa,” she said. It’s the right thing to say in a lighthouse.

Ellis let her put her hand on the brass railing. “You know how this works?” he asked. “It’s not a bulb that shines across the ocean. It’s a steady, stupid little bulb and a bunch of glass that knows how to point. The light would be nothing without the lens.”

She looked at him like he was trying to teach her a lesson, which he was.

“People are like that too,” he said. “We think we have to be brighter. We mostly just need to be better at focusing what we already have.”

She came back the next Tuesday. And the next. Not every time to talk. Sometimes she just did homework on the rocks while he polished. Once she brought him a bad drawing she’d done of the lighthouse. He taped it to the wall next to the official charts.

He never told her to be anything. That was his gift.

Years later, when Ellis died in his sleep, the girl — now a woman living in a city far from any ocean — read about it in the local paper her mother mailed her. She took the train back for the service. There were only nine people there. The new automated light was already doing its job without anyone needing to polish it.

After, she climbed the steps one last time. The Coast Guard officer let her. She stood where she had stood at seventeen and watched the light come on at dusk. It swept out, and swept out, and swept out. Steady. Not trying to do anything except be seen.

She cried, not because Ellis was gone, but because she finally understood what he meant about lonely being a place. She had left it.

I think about that story because I think that’s what words are. Not the light itself. The lens.

We treat words like they are the feeling, but they aren’t. They are the glass we put around the feeling so someone else can see it from far away. Love is not the word “love.” Grief is not the word “grief.” But without the word, how would you signal across the dark water to another ship that you are here, you are here, you are here?

That’s what you’ve given me with these 1000 words. A chance to signal.

If I could use the last of them to tell you anything true, it would be this: You are not behind. You are not too late, too old, too broken to start. The narrative that you missed your chance is a fiction edited to look like a fact. Life isn’t a straight line where you can miss your turn. It’s more like an ocean. You can still change course at any point. You can still head toward a different light.

And you don’t have to be brighter tomorrow. You don’t have to become an entirely new person. You just have to adjust the lens a little. Focus what you already have a bit more carefully. Polish what’s there.

Pay attention to the small, weird miracles that are already yours: the way cold water tastes first thing in the morning, the specific laugh of someone you love, the fact that you can read these words and understand them, the fact that you *feel* anything at all in a universe that is mostly cold rock and burning gas.

It’s absurd that we get to be here. It’s absurd that you are reading this, that I am writing this, that any of this arranged itself into meaning. Don’t get over that.

I have maybe a dozen words left now. I can feel them running out like breath.

So I’ll spend them simply.

Thank you for listening.

If no one has told you today: I’m glad you exist.

Keep your light on.
